source.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some text and figure labels are flattened, but the main results and relevant sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies weight-based analysis to SAE features in Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 language models and reports findings relevant to indirect evidence for SAE features in LLMs; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper measures weight-based token alignment and attention participation of existing SAE features. It does not measure superposition geometry, feature sparsity/co-activation, capacity competition, or whether SAEs recover ground-truth features. Its attention-specialization results concern SAE feature roles not named by the claim versions; these are recorded as findings fitting no version. The paper's statement that feature splitting may explain some lower Llama scores is presented as a hypothesis, not as a separately tested result.
record.test_reason: The paper takes superposition and SAE decomposition as given; its intro states models encode features in superposition. It analyses existing Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAE features with its own weight-based method: logit-lens token coherence and QK attention participation. It does not test whether features are superposed, whether SAEs recover real sparse features, or whether neurons are polysemantic. The ~1/4 'semantic' rate comes from thresholds set at each metric's 50th percentile on one calibration layer. It therefore describes the method's own classification and is not a rate of a phenomenon the claim names. It does not bear on V4 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the authors' third conclusion: semantic coherence and attention participation are inversely related in output-oriented contexts. That relation reverses for input-encoding features in untied-embedding Llama-3.1. The authors also conclude that SAE features show inverted-U attention specialization peaking in mid-layers.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a toy-model superposition experiment: it analyzes pretrained SAE feature weights in Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 through token attribution and QK interactions, rather than testing feature overlap, sparsity, or geometry in controlled toy networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Semantic pass rates depend on model architecture and analysis pairing: Gemma-2 uses tied embeddings, while Llama-3.1 uses separate encoder–embedding and decoder–unembedding analyses. Semantic thresholds are calibrated at selected layers. Attention-specialist rates depend on k and thresholds; the paper also reports effects of excluding self-attention.

fits_no_version.finding: Under percentile-calibrated logit-lens criteria, about 1/4 of SAE features have coherent top tokens. The depth profile is U-shaped in tied-embedding Gemma-2 and bifurcated in untied Llama-3.1 (decoder side rising with depth, encoder side high early).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features' direct token alignment varies with depth and with embedding tying.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-based QK participation of SAE features peaks in middle layers. Query-specialist and key-hub populations depend on depth, model and threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features show depth-dependent, head-partitioned attention specialization in weight-based analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantic features have lower attention weights than non-semantic ones in output-oriented layers (Gemma-2-9B L20: 745 vs 1019). The relation reverses for input-semantic features in Llama-3.1-8B L4 (Fig 7 bottom, semantic higher).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic interpretability and attention participation of SAE features trade off in output-oriented layers but not in input-encoding layers.

record.code_released: The authors state that code will be publicly released, but no URL is stated.
record.problems: The measurements are weight-based and do not use activation data; individual-feature normalization is acknowledged as an approximation to forward-pass normalization. Semantic cutoffs are percentile-based and selected at representative layers. The analysis does not validate SAE feature recovery against ground truth or establish that the feature dictionary is complete or canonical. Some reported layer patterns are described qualitatively rather than with numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the other per-layer semantic pass rates shown only in Figures 3, 4, and 11, or the many per-layer attention plots in Figures 12–14 and 23–34; the paper describes their overall trends but does not give readable numerical values for each layer. Rows R1–R5 preserve the stated aggregate rates and explicitly stated layer-5 result.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
No capacity competition or neuron polysemanticity measured.
No non-capacity causes of polysemanticity examined.
No measure of features spread across neurons, and no test that SAEs recover real or ground-truth sparse features. SAE features are taken as given.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicality. Feature splitting is only hypothesised in Appendix D as a cause of lower Llama rates.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Results not captured as rows: Gemma encoder–embedding averages of 24.66% and 25.16% (Fig 11), and the query-specialist and key-hub threshold sweeps (Tables 1–2; e.g. 53.82% vs 9.75% query specialists at τQ=0.95). Also missing is the Llama L4 reversal (Fig 7 bottom/22b; the text says semantic features weigh higher). These fit no claim version. The feature-splitting explanation for Llama is a hypothesis, not a test of V5.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or overlap geometry is tested.
No test of capacity competition, neuron polysemanticity, or dedication of dimensions to important features.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
The paper analyzes features from existing SAEs in LLMs, but does not test SAE recovery against ground truth or measure how features are distributed across neurons.
No direct test of completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
The analysis treats each SAE feature as a decoder or encoder vector, but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of SAE features passing all three weight-based semantic-coherence thresholds across layers, using decoder–unembedding attribution.

conditions.value: Levenshtein similarity, cosine similarity, and top-100 entropy

rows.measure: Average joint pass rate for features classified as semantically coherent
rows.note: The paper describes the result as an average joint pass rate across layers.
rows.check: Pass rate of the study's own percentile-calibrated token-coherence filter on Gemma-2-2B SAE features. It does not measure feature spreading across neurons or SAE recovery of real features, so it does not bear on V4.

conditions.value: Levenshtein similarity, cosine similarity, and top-100 entropy

rows.measure: Average joint pass rate for features classified as semantically coherent
rows.note: The paper describes the result as an average joint pass rate across layers.
rows.check: Same issue as R1, for Gemma-2-9B. The absolute rate is set largely by the 50th-percentile threshold choice.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of SAE features passing all three weight-based semantic-coherence thresholds.

conditions.value: Levenshtein similarity, cosine similarity, and top-100 entropy

rows.measure: Joint pass rate for features classified as semantically coherent
rows.note: The paper reports this layer-specific rate as an example.
rows.check: Single-layer example (Gemma-2-9B layer 5) of the study's own classifier output. It is not a V4 measure.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of SAE features passing all three weight-based semantic-coherence thresholds using decoder–unembedding attribution.

conditions.value: Levenshtein similarity, cosine similarity, and top-100 entropy

rows.measure: Average joint pass rate for features classified as semantically coherent
rows.value: 23.32%; rate starts near zero in initial layers and rises to over 60% in the final layer
rows.note: The paper reports both the average rate and a monotonic increase with depth.
rows.check: Llama-3.1-8B decoder–unembedding pass rate (23.32%) and its depth profile are method-classification outputs, not V4 evidence.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of SAE features passing all three weight-based semantic-coherence thresholds using encoder–embedding alignment.

conditions.value: Levenshtein similarity, cosine similarity, and top-100 entropy

rows.measure: Average joint pass rate for features classified as semantically coherent
rows.value: 11.82%; rate is exceptionally high in initial layers and becomes negligible after roughly the first third of the model
rows.note: The paper reports a different depth profile for input-space alignment than for decoder–unembedding alignment.
rows.check: The 'partial' state has no basis because no version prediction applies. The row is the study's encoder–embedding classifier output (11.82% average).

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Measured out-of-context pre-softmax attention scores between SAE feature vectors and subsequent-layer QK circuits.
rows.measure: Layerwise pattern of aggregate pre-softmax attention scores
rows.value: Scores are negative in early and late layers and strongly positive in middle layers
rows.note: This reports attention-circuit participation, not overlap geometry or feature recovery.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured out-of-context pre-softmax attention scores between SAE feature vectors and subsequent-layer QK circuits.

conditions.value: absolute magnitude of aggregate attention scores

rows.measure: Layerwise pattern of absolute pre-softmax attention-score magnitude
rows.value: Magnitude follows a low–high–medium pattern and peaks in the middle layers
rows.note: The paper says the signed scores are almost uniformly negative; it interprets their magnitude as having a middle-layer peak.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Counted features meeting post-softmax query-specialist criteria in at least one attention head.
rows.measure: Fraction of features classified as query specialists in any head
rows.note: The paper also reports that excluding self-attention reduces this pass rate, while a significant portion remains.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Counted features meeting post-softmax key-hub criteria in at least one attention head.
rows.measure: Fraction of features classified as key hubs in the any-head union
rows.note: The paper reports an oscillatory layer profile, with peaks in layers 3–10 and 26–32.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared weight-based attention participation distributions of semantic and non-semantic SAE features.

conditions.value: decoder–unembedding semantic classification; query attention weights

rows.measure: Mean aggregate attention weight by feature group
rows.note: The paper reports overlap between distributions, with semantic features shifted toward lower attention weights.
rows.check: The 'population mean' baseline is the mean of a random sample matched in size to the semantic set (n=2,056), not the whole population. The value shown is the query-based measure from Fig 20b.

reader_labels.condition: Weight-based analyses of SAE features in Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B
